title: Devs
synopsis: You took the job because the salary made no sense. The lab is in a sealed building only six people enter. Today they handed you a project and a non-disclosure agreement and a small key.

nodes.text: Forest's hands are soft and his beard is old growth, and the key he gives you is brass, unlabelled, warm from his pocket. The lab sits a mile back into the redwoods behind a fence with no signage on it. 'Devs is the future,' he says. 'You'll love it or you'll quietly leave.' You do the arithmetic on your offer letter. Nobody has quietly left.

choices.text: Accept and ask no further questions
choices.consequence: You sign where the tabs are, all fourteen of them, and skip the clause about post-employment monitoring. The salary is buying that skip and you both know it.

choices.text: Ask one clarifying question
choices.consequence: You ask, and Forest's pause runs a beat long — the pause of a man deciding how much truth a new hire can metabolize.

nodes.text: The floor is a suspended slab; the lab is a building inside a building, wrapped in vacuum and a golden mesh. Six people work at floating consoles and none of them speak. Katie gives you half a smile and no handshake. The hum comes up through your shoes and settles in your back teeth. The air in here has been thinking for years and it shows.

choices.text: Watch what they're doing
choices.consequence: You stand at the back for two hours without being acknowledged, and learn more from the way Lyndon holds his breath than from any line of code.

choices.text: Ask Katie what 'Devs' actually does
choices.consequence: Katie answers in a sentence containing no verbs you recognise, then watches your face to see which word you pick up.

nodes.text: 'Why six?' Forest turns the question over like a stone he found. 'Six is the most people who can keep a secret,' he says, 'and the fewest who can run determinism at this scale.' Behind him a woman crosses the yard carrying nothing. You count her steps to the door — nine — and wonder whether somebody has already counted them for her.

choices.text: Press for what 'determinism' means here
choices.consequence: He says causality is arithmetic with better manners. You nod as though that were an answer, and it goes into you and stays there.

choices.text: File the answer away and start tomorrow
choices.consequence: You let it drop and drive home along the coast with the window down, testing whether wind feels chosen. It doesn't. You start Monday.

nodes.text: Lyndon pulls up a render: a woman in a rough shift, jittering at four frames a second, mouth moving. Audio comes through as a rasp under the noise floor. 'Joan,' he says. 'Fifteenth century. Ten seconds of her.' Nothing recorded this. The machine solved backwards through six hundred years of particle interactions to find her, and she is grainy, and she is turning to look.

choices.text: Believe it and ask how far forward it can read
choices.consequence: You ask how far forward it reaches, and Lyndon grins like a boy holding a firework, and across the room Katie's head comes up from her console.

choices.text: Look for the trick
choices.consequence: You spend a weekend hunting for a rendering pipeline, a training set, any fakery at all. What you find is a machine with no training data, which is worse.

nodes.text: Your badge was printed over someone else's number. Sergei — resigned, went home to Russia, family reasons. Katie tells you this twice in one conversation, arranged two different ways, the way people say a thing they have rehearsed. His locker still holds a jacket and a paper bag of cashews gone soft, and nobody has thought to empty it.

choices.text: Quietly look for Sergei online
choices.consequence: You search his name at home on a phone you've owned since college, and find a Berkeley thesis, a chess rating, and no flight manifest anywhere on earth.

choices.text: Don't look; you want to keep the job
choices.consequence: You close the tab. There is a mortgage, a partner and a visa hanging off this badge, and Sergei is a stranger, and you decide to keep him one.

nodes.text: The coffee shop is loud enough that she has to lean in. Lily — encryption side, Sergei's girlfriend. She has his texts from that last morning, and the punctuation goes wrong halfway down the thread. She isn't crying. She is the kind of frightened that organises: dates, screenshots, a printed map of the campus perimeter. She has more to lose than you do and she came anyway.

choices.text: Help her, carefully
choices.consequence: You give her the shift roster and the gate timings, and from that second you are a person with something to hide inside a building that hides nothing from itself.

choices.text: Plead ignorance and stay safe
choices.consequence: You say you never met him. She thanks you politely and leaves, and you finish a coffee you can no longer taste.

nodes.text: The projection runs ten minutes ahead of the room, rendered in the cube like smoke holding a shape. In it, a cup goes off a cafeteria table at 12:34:06. At 12:34:06 you hear it from two floors down — ceramic, then a laugh. Nobody at the consoles looks up. They stopped finding it remarkable somewhere around month four.

choices.text: Ask if free will exists in this lab
choices.consequence: Stewart answers without turning around: free will is a sensation, not a mechanism. He says it the way you'd hand somebody the wifi password.

choices.text: Ask if it can predict tomorrow
choices.consequence: Tomorrow, they tell you, is nothing special. Resolution falls off with distance, and the distance they actually care about isn't measured in time.

nodes.text: One photograph on the entire floor: a girl, maybe six, mid-sentence on a lawn. Amaya. Forest keeps the frame angled toward his chair, not the door. The rest you get from a decade-old traffic report somebody forgot to scrub — wet on-ramp, hands-free call, his voice in the car at the exact moment of it. This building is a grief with a capital budget.

choices.text: Try to understand Forest's grief
choices.consequence: You start reading everything he does as a man running a conversation backwards. It makes him legible, and legible is not the same thing as safe.

choices.text: Decide grief is making him reckless
choices.consequence: You decide a man who lost a child should not be permitted to own the past tense, and you begin, quietly, keeping notes with timestamps.

nodes.text: Katie waits until Lyndon is on break and the corridor camera has finished its sweep. 'His interpretation is wrong,' she says, close to your ear and not whispering, because whispers carry. 'It isn't one line. It's a sheaf. We render the branch he can stand to watch.' Then she goes back to her console and doesn't speak to you again for nine days.

choices.text: Help Katie argue the many-worlds case
choices.consequence: You run her many-worlds argument at the whiteboard and it holds all the way down, and Forest listens to every word of it and changes nothing.

choices.text: Believe Forest's single-line view
choices.consequence: You take the single line because it's cleaner, and because a universe with one answer in it requires nobody to be brave.

nodes.text: The footage runs thirty-one seconds. Sergei in the parking structure with a phone stuffed in his sock, copying code he barely understood. Kenton comes up behind him — not fast, not angry, simply arriving. Kenton's hands are patient. Afterward he checks his own pulse. Sergei wasn't an asset. He was curious and sloppy, and this company has a body count and a benefits package.

choices.text: Take the evidence to the press
choices.consequence: You mirror the file to a reporter's drop box from a library terminal in Fremont, and walk back out into the sun feeling exactly as safe as you deserve to.

choices.text: Take it to a federal agency
choices.consequence: You take it federal, because federal is slower but carries subpoenas, and slow is a thing you may not personally have much of.

nodes.text: Alone on the platform, you let the visualisations come. Past and future swarm the air in the same golden static. Your own face surfaces out of it. You are on the granite steps outside the lobby, and you are not moving, and there is rain landing on your open eye. The timestamp reads three days from tonight, 6:52 in the evening.

choices.text: Choose to defy the prediction
choices.consequence: You resolve to be elsewhere at 6:52 — another city, another body — and the resolve feels entirely yours, which is precisely what the render predicted it would feel like.

choices.text: Surrender to the determinism
choices.consequence: You stop arguing with the clock and sleep better that night than you have since the offer letter. The comfort of it is the part that frightens Katie.

nodes.text: Level three of a parking structure at three in the morning, engine off, the cabin cooling fast around you. Lily has a cloned badge. Katie has the corridor timings written inside a gum wrapper. You have a hand that won't hold the pen level. Kenton is hunting all three of you, and the entire plan rests on the machine being wrong about one small thing.

choices.text: Execute the plan as written
choices.consequence: You run it to the letter, every mark hit on time, and the eerie part isn't that it works — it's how little of it surprises anybody.

choices.text: Improvise around it
choices.consequence: You throw the script away at the first door and improvise, on the theory that noise is the one commodity determinism cannot purchase.

nodes.text: You walk in without knocking. 'Show me Amaya,' you say. 'The road. All of it.' Forest doesn't ask why. He brings the render up and sits down on the floor beneath it like a man at a graveside, and you watch eight seconds of wet asphalt at a resolution no father should be permitted to own. Then you are both crying about entirely different things.

choices.text: Stay and help him let it go
choices.consequence: You stay, and begin the slow work of talking a man down off a machine — harder than it sounds, because the machine keeps agreeing with him.

choices.text: Stay and help him keep it on
choices.consequence: You stay, and hand him the tissue, and say nothing whatsoever about switching it off. The lab has just acquired its seventh believer.

nodes.text: The prediction put this at 9:41 and it is 9:41. Kenton comes down the corridor at a walk, unhurried, a man arriving at an appointment. You and Lily take the service elevator and his fingers make it through the closing doors — four of them, flat, white at the knuckle — and then don't. Above you the cube hums on, having already watched all of this.

choices.text: Reach the top and confront Forest
choices.consequence: You go up, because Forest is the only person who can stop the building, and because some part of you wants to be looked at by him one last time.

choices.text: Go to the basement and pull the plug
choices.consequence: You go down, toward concrete and cold, where the answer is a switch instead of a conversation you'd have to win.

nodes.text: Katie writes the code out longhand rather than send it anywhere. 'Forty-seven seconds to unwind,' she says. 'It knows inside the first one.' She doesn't specify who 'it' is. Your palms are damp on the console rail. Overhead the lattice is already rendering the next minute, and somewhere in that minute a pair of hands is moving exactly the way yours are about to.

choices.text: Begin the sequence anyway
choices.consequence: You start it anyway and the counter runs, and knowing you were always going to press it does absolutely nothing to slow your heart.

choices.text: Hesitate for a second of free will
choices.consequence: You hold for one second — deliberate, useless, gorgeous — and Katie looks at you as though you have just proved her entire case for her.

nodes.text: Forest waits by the glass with his hands loose at his sides. No guards. He doesn't move when you come in. 'I'm not going to fight you,' he says, and he means it, and it is not kindness. He wants a choice made, tonight: render Amaya into the cube and live inside it, or let this version of him stop at the bottom of a stairwell.

choices.text: Render his daughter
choices.consequence: You reach for the console, and Forest shuts his eyes like a man being told the anaesthetic has started working.

choices.text: Refuse and walk him out
choices.consequence: You take his elbow and walk him toward the elevator, and feel through the sleeve how little of him is left to walk anywhere.

nodes.text: Twelve metres down, in a chamber the size of a chapel, the hardware hangs in vacuum a few thousandths of a degree above nothing at all. Cold radiates off the glass and makes your eyes water. The kill switch is a red mushroom head on a keyed stalk, mounted at chest height by somebody who very sincerely hoped no one would ever reach for it.

choices.text: Pull the switch and end it
choices.consequence: The stalk takes more force than you expect, and the hum drops octave by octave until the room is just a room with an expensive refrigerator in it.

choices.text: Walk away without pulling it
choices.consequence: You put your hand back in your pocket and climb the stairs, and the machine goes on being right about everything, including you.

nodes.text: The lattice brightens until the walls stop existing. A girl runs across a lawn toward a screen door with a repaired hinge, and the light on the grass is the exact light of one afternoon eight summers ago. Forest is down on the floor watching her, smiling — you have never seen him do it, and it is unbearable. Then the room comes apart into two rooms.

choices.text: Stay in the rendered universe with Lily
choices.consequence: You step through with Lily into a world that has a sun in it, knowing every photon of that sun has an author.

choices.text: Stay in the unrendered universe and live
choices.consequence: You stay where the coffee is bad and the light belongs to nobody, and let the other two of you go on without you.

nodes.text: The lab is sealed and the redwoods get their fence back. Forest dies at the foot of the stairs at the hour he was told he would. Lily doesn't, which is the only thing the machine got wrong all night. A campus guard puts his jacket around your shoulders outside. The street is wet and ordinary and nobody anywhere is rendering it. You walk.

choices.text: Testify in the federal inquiry
choices.consequence: You keep every timestamp and badge log and hand it to people with subpoena power, and forfeit any future life in which nobody knows your name.

choices.text: Disappear and rebuild
choices.consequence: You sell the car, kill the numbers, and go somewhere the word 'quantum' only ever turns up in advertising for mattresses.

nodes.text: Years on, a coffee shop in a city that has weather. You flip a quarter twenty times across the table because you still do this, the way other people touch a doorframe on the way out. Thirteen heads. None of it means anything, which is precisely the point you drove across a state to make to yourself. The barista asks if it's for here. It is.

choices.text: Live the rest of your life unmeasured
choices.consequence: You leave the coin on the table for whoever sits down next and go home to a life with no logging in it.

choices.text: Write a memoir about Devs, carefully
choices.consequence: You start writing it slowly, with a lawyer's number saved in your phone and every name changed except the one they'd recognise anyway.

nodes.text: You and Lily live inside a solved universe. The coffee is hot at the temperature coffee is hot. The sun goes down the way that sun went down. Somewhere in a house with a repaired hinge, Amaya grows up, gets bored, gets a job, gets old — an entire life priced in electricity. Nothing here is less true than anything else; it simply has an author. One morning you stop asking, and find that you can breathe.

You come out into a Tuesday the machine never finished computing, and the sky over the parking lot is the same dull white it would have been regardless. Lily takes your hand at the crosswalk. Forest went down those stairs on a schedule that was never yours to interrupt. Nothing about the morning is remarkable in any direction. You had forgotten how much you liked that.

Six weeks of testimony, three engineers charged, one company dissolved into other companies with cleaner names. Then the part nobody films: two years later a lab in Shenzhen publishes the same architecture with a friendlier acronym. You write the memoir anyway — careful, dull in the right places, honest about the week you decided not to look for Sergei. It's assigned in ethics seminars at three universities now, and the students argue about you in the present tense.

A small city, a job with a timesheet, a flat above a laundromat that shudders at nine every night. When the documentary airs you are at the corner store buying oranges, and you never watch it, not even the segment where they blur your face. The oranges are exactly as orange as oranges. You peel one on the walk home and the smell gets under your thumbnail and stays there for hours, and nobody anywhere predicted that.
